summary: Gives guidelines to help authors of RTP payload format specifications make good design choices. It is a Best Current Practice.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2736 gives design guidance for RTP media payloads. Its main goal is to keep each received packet useful even when earlier packets are lost or delayed.

questions: how to write an rtp payload format
why avoid ip fragmentation for rtp
how should an rtp payload handle packet loss
subtitle: Design RTP payloads so received packets remain useful when other packets are lost.

tldr.problem: RTP packets can be lost, duplicated, reordered, or fragmented. A payload format that splits meaningful codec data across packets can make additional received data unusable after a loss.
tldr.mechanism: The guidelines recommend packet boundaries that match codec frames, payloads that can be processed independently, and format-specific fragmentation rather than reliance on IP fragmentation.
tldr.outcome: The recommendations help payload formats remain useful on best-effort networks. RFC 2736 is BCP 36 and has been updated by RFC 8088.

today: RFC 2736 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 36) published in December 1999. It has been updated by RFC 8088.

sections.title: Purpose of the Guidelines
sections.content:
RFC 2736 gives guidance to authors of Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) payload formats. A payload format describes how a codec's data is carried in RTP packets. The advice applies broadly, with audio and video codecs used for examples.

The recommendations reflect experience designing RTP formats for networks where packet loss and delay can occur.
sections.plainLanguage: This document helps authors decide how to place codec data in RTP packets. It focuses on designs that still work when the network loses or delays packets.

sections.title: Application-Level Framing
sections.content:
RTP follows Application-Level Framing: the application can decide how to handle a lost or late unit of data. An Application Data Unit (ADU) is a unit the receiver can process without waiting for other ADUs. It should carry enough information to identify its place in the media.

RTP's header can identify a packet regardless of order or earlier loss, but the payload format must also support independent processing. The endpoints should adapt transmission to the network's limits.
sections.plainLanguage: A packet should carry enough information for the receiver to use it without waiting for missing packets. The payload format must support that, not just the RTP header.

sections.title: Loss, Fragmentation, and Jitter
sections.content:
In best-effort RTP over UDP/IP, packets may be lost, duplicated, or reordered. A packet larger than the network's Maximum Transmission Unit may be fragmented. If one fragment is lost, the receiver discards the other fragments of that packet, wasting bandwidth and processing.

Packet transit time also varies because of queueing and route changes. A playout buffer can help with some timing variation, but route changes are harder to predict and handle.
sections.plainLanguage: Packets may arrive late, more than once, or not at all. If the network splits a large packet and loses one fragment, the remaining fragments cannot restore it.

sections.title: Keep Packets Useful
sections.content:
Payload formats should remain useful when a moderate amount of packet loss occurs. Ideally, each packet can be decoded even if earlier packets were lost or are late. The RFC notes that a 5% loss rate is not uncommon on the public Internet.

Packet boundaries should align with codec-frame boundaries, and a codec's smallest meaningful unit should not cross a packet boundary unless it is larger than the MTU. If a frame exceeds the MTU, the payload format should define its own fragmentation method instead of relying on IP fragmentation.
sections.plainLanguage: Put complete codec frames in packets so the receiver can use each packet on its own. If a frame is too large, define how to split it instead of relying on the network.

sections.title: Codec State and Payload Details
sections.content:
Some codecs use decoder state that tracks the encoder. After a lost packet, later frames may be decoded but sound distorted while the decoder catches up. The RFC recommends considering a small header with the most important state information to reduce the distortion.

Codec parameters can be signaled before transmission, changed out of band during a session, indicated by a payload type, or carried in the payload. Mid-session out-of-band changes need synchronization. Payload-specific information generally belongs in the payload, not an RTP header extension.
sections.plainLanguage: Some codecs need earlier information to decode later frames accurately. A small amount of state in each packet can reduce distortion after a loss.

sections.title: Compression and Parameter Trade-Offs
sections.content:
RTP header compression works best when timestamps increase by a constant amount between packets. Formats that send packets out of order may compress less efficiently, so designers should consider alternatives where possible.

Putting a codec parameter in every payload can make a format more adaptable but less efficient. The format designer must weigh that cost against the need to change the parameter during a session.
sections.plainLanguage: Some packet choices make headers harder to compress. A designer should compare that cost with the benefit of sending packets out of order or changing parameters.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Formats designed for networks with almost no loss may be more fragile and easier targets for denial-of-service attacks. Designers should define how implementations handle illegal values and mismatches between length fields and actual data; discarding a malformed packet is usually appropriate.

Adding forward error correction automatically after loss can increase congestion and worsen the loss. A payload format that does this should include safeguards against abuse. Encryption of RTP payloads is covered by RTP, though a format may affect where encryption keys can safely change.
sections.plainLanguage: Define what to do with malformed packets and avoid responses that add too much traffic. Extra recovery data can increase congestion if senders add it without limits.
